text: Sreeja is a Research Assistant at DePaul University (Sep 2025 to present), working on harmonic persistence barcodes for machine learning. Her research sits at the intersection of topology and machine learning. Topological data analysis studies the shape of data: loops, voids, and connected components that survive across scales. She works on harmonic persistence barcodes, a way of enriching these topological signatures with geometric information carried by harmonic chains. Concretely, she implements matrix-based algorithms in Python that turn mathematical specifications into clean, tested code, and runs experiments comparing these enriched barcodes against traditional persistence features on shape classification tasks. Early results are promising, and a publication is in preparation. The code is private while the work is under way, but she's happy to talk about it in detail. Related tools/topics: Topological Data Analysis, Persistent Homology, GUDHI, Linear Algebra, Python. Alongside her research, she builds live products such as WanderWear, an AI travel planner and personal stylist running in production on AWS.
short: Right now she's a Research Assistant at DePaul working on harmonic persistence barcodes, a way to make topological data analysis carry richer geometric information. topic: WanderWear challenges hardest hard problem difficult tough what did she learn lessons learned takeaways bugs engineering story
short: Two stand out. First, the cloud gateway cuts off any request after 30 seconds, but planning a trip can take longer, so she redesigned planning as background jobs the app checks on. That also made it scale. Second, during testing before launch she found that a new account could see another account's saved outfits. She traced it to three separate issues lining up, fixed all three, and added tests so it can never come back.
text: What did Sreeja learn from building WanderWear, and what were the hardest problems? First, the cloud gateway cuts off any request after 30 seconds, but planning a trip can take longer, so she redesigned trip planning as background jobs that the app checks on, which also made the service scale. Second, during testing before launch she found that a newly created account could see another account's saved outfits. She traced the problem to three separate issues lining up, fixed all three, and added automated tests so that kind of data leak can never come back. Her lessons: design around real limits, and never trust a fix without a test that proves it.
